The South African veteran (27) has been the most consistent 400m runner on the circuit in early 2026. He has also been a powerhouse in the 4x400m relay, anchoring South Africa to silver at the World Relays (2:55.07). While he lacks the raw 43‑second potential of Kebinatshipi and Morales Williams, his form curve is rising. A **44.24** would be a season’s best and likely enough for the podium, but he may be edged by the two younger stars with higher ceilings.

Ndori won the 2025 Xiamen Diamond League in **44.25** and took bronze at the World Championships (44.20). His 2026 season has been steady but not spectacular: **44.62** at the Botswana Championships (4 April) and relay duties at the World Relays. He will likely run a well‑judged race from the front, but the depth of the field means he might slip to 4th. A **44.32** is a realistic improvement on his seasonal best.

Samukonga’s consistency over the past two years has been borderline sub‑45, but he rarely dips below 44.40. In this loaded field, he will probably settle for a mid‑44.4 performance, around **44.48**.

#### 6. Chris Bailey – 44.55
The American (25) is the World Indoor champion (2025) and a 4x400m Olympic gold medallist, but his 2026 outdoor season has been modest. He ran **44.60** at the Arkansas Twilight on 8 May, his only 400m of note. In 2025, he won the Xiamen Diamond League in 44.27 and the Shaoxing meet in 44.17, so he knows how to win here. However, he has not yet recaptured that form. His 200m times (20.72) suggest he is still building, and he may lack the finishing gear needed to stay with the leaders. A **44.55** is consistent with his recent output.

#### 7. Vernon Norwood – 44.68
At 33, Norwood is the oldest in the field but remains a relay legend with four Olympic medals. His 2026 outdoor best is **44.58** (Mt. SAC Relays, 18 April), but he faded to 45.22 in Tokyo on 17 May, indicating a dip in form. He was 4th at the London Diamond League last year (44.34) and 2nd in Brussels (44.62), so he can still produce a strong race. However, the younger athletes have more speed and endurance at this stage of the season. Expect a solid but not spectacular **44.68**.

#### 8. Attila Molnár – 45.15
The Hungarian (23) set the indoor European record of 45.01 in February 2026 and won European indoor gold, but his 2026 outdoor campaign is still nascent. He has not raced a single outdoor 400m this year based on the provided data; his last outdoor race was 44.74 in August 2025. The transition from indoor to outdoor often takes time, and he may lack the rhythm and top‑end speed required to challenge the elite here. His indoor final at the World Indoors (45.71) suggests he is not yet in sub‑45 outdoor shape. A debut outdoor time around **45.15** would be a solid opening.

#### 9. Kai Liu – 45.85
The 19‑year‑old Chinese prodigy is the clear underdog. His best 400m is 45.06 from the 2025 Chinese Championships, but his 2026 outdoor best is only **46.10** (April). Competing against a world‑class field on home soil will be a valuable experience, but he is likely to finish well behind the pack. A time near **45.85** would be a respectable improvement on his season’s best.

- **Samukonga, Bailey, Norwood** are well‑matched but behind the top four.

The race will likely be decided on the final straight, with Morales Williams’ early‑season sharpness prevailing over Kebinatshipi’s raw talent. Nene will hold on for bronze, while Ndori and Samukonga round out the top five.

Furlani enters as the reigning outdoor and indoor world champion (2025), a status he cemented with a dominant 8.39 m to win gold at the Tokyo World Championships. His recent form is staggering: just one week before this meet (16 May 2026), he won the Shaoxing Diamond League promotional event with a huge **8.43 m (+0.4 m/s)** – the best outdoor mark of the year by any athlete. He also posted **8.39 m indoors in February 2026**, showing he carries indoor momentum outdoors. At 20, he is the youngest in the field but has proven he can handle pressure and big stages. His consistency is unmatched: five of his last six competitions have been 8.30 m or better. The Xiamen crowd will be lively, but Furlani thrives in high-quality fields. He is the clear favourite.

**2. Bozhidar Sarâboyukov (BUL, 21 years old)**  
The Bulgarian sensation has been the most improved jumper globally. He won the 2025 European Indoor gold and then took bronze at the 2026 World Indoor Championships (8.31 m indoors). His indoor campaign included a stunning **8.45 m in Belgrade (Feb 2026)** – the best indoor mark in the world this season. Outdoors, he placed 2nd in Shaoxing (8.07 m) but that was a rare off-day; his raw talent suggests he will bounce back. He also topped the 2025 World Championships final (5th, 8.19 m) and has beaten Tentoglou, Gayle, and Pinnock head-to-head this year. He is still refining his run-up but has the top-end speed and pop to challenge Furlani. Expect a big leap here, possibly his first outdoor 8.30 m.

**3. Wayne Pinnock (JAM, 25 years old)**  
Pinnock is a serial big-meet performer: Olympic silver (2024), World Championships silver (2023), World Indoor silver (2025). However, his 2026 outdoors has been quiet – he placed only 7th in Shaoxing (7.93 m) and has yet to break 8.10 m this season outdoors. That said, he has a history of rising to Diamond League occasions: he won the London DL in 2025 (8.20 m) and placed 4th in Zürich (8.15 m). He has the second-best peak (8.29 m indoor) in the field after Furlani. His technical savvy and ability to produce a clutch jump under pressure make him a podium threat. He should improve his 2026 outdoor best here.

**4. Yuhao Shi (CHN, 27 years old)**  
Home favourite Shi was the bronze medallist at the 2025 World Championships in Tokyo, jumping **8.33 m** – a massive personal breakthrough on the global stage. He has struggled to replicate that form in 2026, with a best of 8.14 m (windy) and a no-mark in Shaoxing. However, Xiamen is a familiar venue (he jumped 8.08 m here in 2025), and he always raises his game in China. His technical consistency is solid, and he is a proven championship performer. He looked vulnerable at the end of 2025, with two sub-7.70 m jumps in Lausanne and Zürich. At 27, he is still young but seems to be struggling with a run-up rhythm or motivation. He has the talent to win any meet, but recent data suggests he is no longer the dominant force. A mid-8.10s jump would be a solid comeback, but he will not beat Furlani or Sarâboyukov in this form.

The 2019 world champion is past his prime. He has not jumped over 8.15 m outdoors since 2021 and was only 7th at the 2025 World Championships (7.86 m). His 2026 best is 8.11 m in a low-key US meet. He was 6th in Shaoxing (7.93 m) and 4th at the 2026 World Indoor Championships (8.12 m). At 29, he still has experience, but he no longer poses a threat to the podium. A top-8 finish would be a success.

**9. Heng Shu (CHN, 21 years old)**  
The 2025 Asian champion (8.22 m) has struggled in 2026, with a best of only 8.01 m outdoors and a poor 13th at World Indoors (7.76 m). He is young and still learning, but he looks a step behind the world leaders right now.

**10. Anvar Anvarov (UZB, 25 years old)**  
Anvarov is the Uzbek record holder (8.25 m) but has not reproduced that form often. He was 3rd in Shaoxing (8.01 m) and has a best of 8.09 m in 2025. He is a solid competitor but lacks the explosiveness to crack 8.10 m consistently.

- **The Furlani Factor**: At 20, Furlani has already beaten every athlete in this field in the last 12 months. His 8.43 m in Shaoxing is a clear warning shot. Expect him to put down a big first-round mark and dare others to chase.
- **Sarâboyukov’s Ceiling**: He has the best indoor mark in the world this year (8.45 m) and is the only athlete who has matched Furlani’s raw distance potential. If he gets a good wind, he could push Furlani to 8.45+.
- **Pinnock’s Clutch Reputation**: He tends to jump his best in the final rounds. Look for him to improve after a conservative start.
- **Home Advantage for China**: Shi and Zhang will have crowd support, but neither has beaten Furlani or Sarâboyukov head-to-head recently.

**Predicted Winning Mark**: **8.41 m** – a world lead and a statement from the young Italian champion. The battle for silver and bronze will be fierce, but Sarâboyukov’s indoor fireworks suggest he is ready to break through outdoors.

5. **Shaunae Miller-Uibo** (BAH) – **22.46** (+0.2 m/s)
6. **Jenna Prandini** (USA) – **22.68** (+0.2 m/s)
7. **Yujie Chen** (CHN) – **22.85** (+0.2 m/s)
8. **Mckenzie Long** (USA) – **22.92** (+0.2 m/s)
9. **Torrie Lewis** (AUS) – **23.28** (+0.2 m/s)

### Race Preview & Reasoning

The Xiamen 200 m brings together a mix of proven champions, emerging stars, and athletes seeking redemption. The data from the 2025–2026 season provides a clear hierarchy, with Shericka Jackson, the second-fastest woman in history over 200 m, as the overwhelming favourite. However, the depth of the field means the battle for the podium will be fierce.

**Shericka Jackson** enters as the only woman in the field with a sub-22-second legal performance in the past year (21.99 in the 2025 World Championships semi-final). Her 22.07 victory in Shaoxing (16 May 2026) – the most recent 200 m outing for most of this field – was the fastest of any competitor that day and came with a controlled, effortless style. Even at 31, Jackson’s blend of top-end speed and curve-running technique remains unmatched. Her ability to go 22.17 in Chorzów (August 2025) and 22.07 in Shaoxing suggests she is peaking perfectly for this early-season Diamond League swing. The only minor concern is her fourth-place finish in the 100 m at the 2025 World Championships (10.88), but her 200 m consistency—winning her semi-final in 21.99 and taking bronze in the final (22.18)—proves she can deliver when it matters. Expect Jackson to control the race from the gun and close hard.

**Anavia Battle** has been the most consistent 200 m performer outside of Jackson over the past 12 months. She won the 200 m at the 2025 Xiamen Diamond League (22.41), the Shaoxing Diamond League (22.38), the Golden Gala (22.53), and the Meeting de Paris (22.27). More impressively, she placed 2nd at the 2025 US Championships (22.13) and 4th at the World Championships final (22.22) – meaning she finished higher than any other American in this race at those two major meets. Her 22.40 in Shaoxing (16 May 2026) was her third consecutive Diamond League race under 22.45. Battle’s ability to produce fast times in back-to-back meets, her strong curve, and her tactical maturity make her the clear second favourite. She will likely push Jackson through the first 100 m and hold off the chasing pack.

**Amy Hunt** is the rising star of British sprinting. At just 23, she already owns a World Championships silver medal in the 200 m (22.14 in Tokyo 2025) and a 60 m indoor best of 7.04 (Toruń, Feb 2026) that signals exceptional speed endurance. Her semi-final at the 2025 World Championships (22.08) was faster than any woman in this field except Jackson’s 21.99. Hunt’s 2025 season was a breakout: she beat several of these rivals in Paris (22.45, 2nd) and London (22.31, 3rd), and she won the UK title over 100 m (11.02). Her 22.48 in Shaoxing (16 May) was a slight step back, but that race came after a heavy indoor season and a transatlantic flight. With a week to adjust, Hunt’s turn of foot and improving strength should see her edge out the more experienced Richardson and Miller-Uibo for the bronze.

**Sha'Carri Richardson** remains an enigma. Her 100 m pedigree is undeniable (10.72 personal best, 5th at the 2025 World Championships), but her 200 m consistency has lagged behind. Her 22.42 in Shaoxing was her fastest outdoor 200 m since the 2023 season and a clear step in the right direction after a 2025 campaign where she struggled to break 22.5 (22.56 at US Trials, 22.42 in Shaoxing). However, she has not won a 200 m Diamond League race since 2023, and her performances against this specific field have been uneven: she was 4th in Shaoxing, 6th in the 100 m at the 2025 Silesia meet, and failed to make the 200 m final at the 2025 World Championships. Richardson’s explosive start is a weapon, but her ability to hold form over the final 50 metres against athletes like Battle and Hunt remains a question mark. She should be in the mix for 4th, but a podium finish would require a season-best performance.

**Shaunae Miller-Uibo** is a two-time Olympic 400 m champion transitioning back to the 200 m after years of focusing on the longer sprint. Her 2026 outdoor opener was strong: 22.44 at the Florida Relays and 22.26 in Shaoxing (2nd place). That Shaoxing time was her fastest 200 m since 2022 and suggests she is rounding into form. However, Miller-Uibo’s resume is built on the 400 m, and her 200 m tactics often involve a patient first half followed by a furious finish – a strategy that works well against less experienced runners but can leave her vulnerable to faster starters like Jackson and Battle. Her 2025 season was interrupted by injury (she DNS'd the NACAC 400 m final), and she spent much of the year running 100 m and 200 m in lower-level meets (11.68 in Poland). The Xiamen field is much deeper than those races. She can challenge for 4th or 5th, but her lack of recent high-pressure 200 m wins over this calibre of runner drops her outside the podium.

**Jenna Prandini** is the wily veteran of the field (33) and a two-time Olympian. She has shown flashes of form in 2026: 22.36 (-0.1) in Tucson and 22.43 (+3.3 wind-aided) at Mt. SAC. However, her legal-season bests have been less impressive: 22.68 in Shaoxing (16 May) and 22.78 in Chorzów (2025). Prandini’s consistency and experience are assets, but she no longer possesses the raw speed to challenge the top four. She will likely run a steady race, slot into 6th, and be content with a solid Diamond League points haul.

**Yujie Chen** is just 17 years old but already the Asian 100 m champion and Chinese national champion. Her 200 m best of 22.84 (Shaoxing, 16 May) is a remarkable time for her age, but she is still learning to compete against world-class fields. She ran 23.02 to win the National Games in November 2025, and her 22.84 in Shaoxing was a clear personal best. However, the intensity of the Diamond League environment and the caliber of her rivals – many of whom are full-time professionals with years of experience in high-pressure finals – will be a significant challenge. She should improve on her 2025 Xiamen run (22.99) but will likely fade in the final 50 m against more powerful athletes.

**Mckenzie Long** had a breakthrough 2025 season, winning the Ed Murphey Classic (21.93 legal) and making the World Championships semi-finals. However, her 2026 campaign has been disastrous: she finished 8th in Shaoxing (22.85) and 3rd at the USA Indoor Championships (60 m, 7.20). Her 22.85 in Shaoxing was nearly a full second slower than her personal best, and she has not broken 22.4 outdoors in 2026. The inconsistency that plagued her at the World Championships (8th in the final) seems to have carried over. She has the raw talent to run 22.0, but her recent form suggests she will struggle to match the likes of Hunt, Battle, and even Prandini.

**Torrie Lewis** is the youngest athlete in the field (20) and the reigning Australian 100/200 m champion. However, her 2026 season has been a struggle: she finished 9th in Shaoxing (23.25) and has not broken 22.8 outdoors this year. Her 2025 World Championships showed promise (22.56 in the heats), but she was well off the pace in the semi-finals (22.69). The Australian has good speed endurance (7.14 indoor 60 m) but seems to be struggling to translate that to outdoor 200 m success against elite competition. She will likely trail the field but gain invaluable experience.

**Conclusion:** Jackson’s class and recent form make her a near-certain winner. Battle’s consistency and proven Diamond League pedigree earn her silver. Hunt’s upward trajectory and world-class 200 m semi-final time give her the edge over the fading Miller-Uibo and the erratic Richardson. The rest of the field will be fighting for minor placings.

### Reasoning & Analysis

**1. Valarie Sion**  
The reigning Olympic and World champion is the clear favorite. Her 2026 campaign already features a monumental 73.10 m win in Oklahoma (11 April) – the second-best mark of her career – and she defeated van Klinken head-to-head there by more than two meters. Even a rare sixth-place finish (65.18 m) earlier in April looks like an outlier; she has since rebounded emphatically. At 30, Sion is at her peak, and her consistency in the 68–73 m range over the past two years (including a 2025 World gold of 69.48 m) makes her the overwhelming choice to win in Xiamen.

**2. Jorinde van Klinken**  
The Dutch record holder (70.99 m, set in the same Oklahoma meet where Sion threw 73.10) is in superb early-season form. Her 68.98 m win on 9 April and 70.99 m runner-up finish on 11 April show she is capable of pushing Sion. However, she has never beaten Sion in a Diamond League or global final (she was second at the 2025 Worlds with 67.50 m, and fourth in Xiamen last year). She will likely settle for silver again, but her recent trajectory suggests she could threaten 70 m again.

**3. Cierra Jackson**  
The 2025 NCAA champion and rising American star threw 67.25 m on 11 April (Oklahoma Throws Series), finishing fourth behind Sion, van Klinken, and Fraley. That mark is superior to anything posted by the athletes ranked below her in this prediction. At 23, she is improving rapidly; she also placed second at the 2025 Prefontaine Classic (67.82 m) and fifth at the Diamond League final in Zürich (64.40 m). Her consistency in the 64–67 m range and youthful momentum give her an edge over the more experienced but slightly less explosive Craft and Beistle.

**4. Erika Beistle**  
A Division II standout, Beistle has been on a tear in 2026, throwing 66.72 m on 10 May at a GVSU meet – her personal best and the highest mark of any non-Sion/van Klinken American this year. She also recorded 66.34 m on 3 April and 65.57 m on 24 April. While she lacks top-level Diamond League experience, her recent form is undeniable. She overtakes Craft because her 66.72 m is a better peak than Craft’s best 2026 mark of 66.03 m, and she is trending upward.

**5. Shanice Craft**  
The German veteran is a model of consistency, with a 2026 best of 66.03 m (14 May) and a 65.21 m win the following day. She placed eighth at the 2025 Worlds (65.21 m) and has a career high of 68.10 m from 2025. Craft is reliable but lacks the ceiling of the younger Americans; she rarely exceeds 66 m now at age 32. She should hold off Feng but will struggle to match the explosiveness of Jackson or Beistle.

**6. Bin Feng**  
The 2022 world champion and 2024 Olympic silver medalist has been steady if unspectacular in 2026, winning a Chinese Grand Prix with 63.28 m on 9 May. Her personal best (69.12 m) is still strong, but she has not approached 67 m since 2022. Her 2025 season included a 65.28 m seventh-place finish at Worlds. She is a podium contender only if others falter; here she lands sixth due to her reliable 63–64 m base.

**7. Laulauga Tausaga**  
Tausaga is a major question mark. The 2023 world champion (69.49 m) and holder of a 70.72 m PB in 2025 has been well below that level in 2026, with bests of 62.87 m and 62.31 m in her two outings. Her 2025 season was also inconsistent – she placed sixth at Worlds (65.49 m) and had several sub-63 m performances. Until she shows a return to 67 m+ form, she cannot be ranked higher.

**8. Veronica Fraley**  
Fraley has talent (68.72 m PB from 2025) but lacks reliability. Her 2026 results include a 67.01 m fifth-place in Oklahoma (11 April) but also a 60.76 m on 16 May. She is capable of a big throw but is equally likely to miss the mark. She tends to struggle in high-pressure Diamond League settings (e.g., 10th in Paris 2025, 6th at USATF Throws Festival). Eighth place feels appropriate.

**9. Silinda Moráles**  
The Cuban bronze medalist at the 2025 Worlds (67.25 m) has not replicated that form in 2026. Her best this year is 63.86 m (February), and her most recent meet (20 February) was only 60.30 m. She has not faced top international competition since last summer and may lack the sharpness to contend for a top-six finish.

**10. Vanessa Kamga**  
Kamga set her PB of 66.61 m at the 2025 Worlds (fourth place), but her 2026 season has been modest. A 58.82 m at the European Throwing Cup (15 March) and a 59.02 m in early May suggest she is a long way from peak shape. She finished ninth in Xiamen last year (59.88 m) and is likely to repeat a similar result.

### Race Preview & Reasoning

**Top Contenders**  
The race revolves around two men in scintillating form: Andreas Almgren and Mohamed Abdilaahi. Both ran outstanding 3000m races at the Shaoxing Diamond League on 16 May 2026 – Abdilaahi won in 7:25.77, Almgren was second in 7:26.48. That 3000m is the best recent gauge of speed endurance, and both are proven 5000m runners. Almgren holds the European record of 12:44.27 (BAUHAUS-Galan 2025) and has shown incredible consistency on the road (26:45 10K in January 2026). Abdilaahi, on the other hand, set a German 10,000m record (26:56.58) in March 2026 and has a 5000m best of 12:53.63 (Monaco 2025). His 3000m victory – by nearly a second over Almgren – signals superior current sharpness. However, Almgren’s proven ability over the full 5000m distance and his European record pedigree give him the edge to hold off Abdilaahi in a tactical, fast finish.

**The Young Ethiopian Threat**  
Biniam Mehary (19) did not race in Shaoxing, but his 2025 credentials are frightening: he ran 12:45.93 in Oslo (2nd) and placed 5th in the World Championships final (12:59.95). He also set a world U20 record in the indoor 3000m. His absence from the Shaoxing meet suggests possible rest or preparation for Xiamen. With his raw speed and endurance, he should push the leaders early, but his lack of a recent sharp race might cost him a place behind the two in-form veterans.

**The Miler’s Gamble**  
Timothy Cheruiyot, a 1500m Olympic silver medallist, surprised many by running 7:27.24 for 3000m in Shaoxing (4th). He rarely contests the 5000m, but his 1500m speed (3:29.75 in 2025) and strong recent form make him a dangerous wildcard. He will likely try to stay close and use a final kick. However, his endurance over 12.5 laps is unproven at this level – his best 5000m is probably around 13:10. He’ll fade slightly from the top three but still outkick the next tier.

**The Kenyan Pack and Others**  
Cornelius Kemboi (5th in Shaoxing 3000m, 7:27.46), Eduardo Herrera (7th, 7:27.63), and Mathew Kipchumba Kipsang (6th, 7:27.58) form a very tight group. All have 5000m PBs in the 12:57‑12:59 range. Kemboi won the Kip Keino Classic 5000m in April (13:09.31), while Herrera is a Mexican record holder (12:58.57) and Kipsang is a strong cross-country runner with 12:58.61 speed. They lack the top-end gear of Almgren, Abdilaahi, or Mehary and will battle for places 5‑7. Birhanu Balew (12th in Shaoxing, 7:29.60) is a former 12:48 runner but his recent form has dipped – a 58:23 half marathon in February suggests good base, but the track speed is lagging. Jacob Krop (8th in Shaoxing, 7:28.72) has been inconsistent since his 2022‑23 medal days; he’s not the same force.

**Midfield & Lower Tier**  
Addisu Yihune and Mezgebu Sime are both 20‑22 years old with 5000m bests around 13:00‑13:04, but they haven’t raced a 5000m track in 2026 and their recent road 5K times (13:14‑13:21) don’t translate to elite track speed. Seth O’Donnell (11th in Shaoxing 3000m, 7:29.49) continues to improve – he won the Australian 5000m title in 13:12.42 – but is still a step below the top Africans. Santiago Catrofe, Khairi Bejiga, Harbert Kibet, Edwin Kurgat, Keneth Kiprop, and Tim Verbaandert all finished outside the top 10 in Shaoxing’s 3000m, indicating they lack the necessary base or sharpness for a fast 5000m. Kiprop (7:33.70) was especially disappointing after his 13:00.49 in 2025. Abdisa Fayisa (19th in 7:36.73) and Filip Sasínek (DNF) are not in form, while Boaz Kiprugut has a long list of recent DNFs and is unlikely to finish.

**Pacing & Tactics**  
Given the depth of talent, expect a quick early pace – likely through 3000m in ~7:50‑7:55. The Shaoxing 3000m winner Abdilaahi and European record‑holder Almgren will drive it. Mehary and Cheruiyot will stay in contact. The final 1000m will see Almgren’s superior 5000m expertise and Abdilaahi’s raw strength decide the winner. A sub‑12:50 is very probable, with the top three all under 12:52. The race will be a fascinating clash of a European record‑holder, a German national record‑holder, an Ethiopian teenage prodigy, and an Olympic medallist stepping up in distance.

**Race Preview & Analysis**

**The Contenders**

This 1500m field is exceptionally deep, featuring the reigning World Championship silver and bronze medallists, the World U20 record holder, and a host of sub-4:00 performers from the 2025 season. The key to the prediction lies in recent form from the Shaoxing Diamond League on 16 May 2026 (just one week prior) and the athletes' overall momentum heading into late May.

**Race Shape & Tactical Expectations**

The Egret Stadium in Xiamen typically produces fast, honest races. With no clear front-runner willing to gamble from the gun, the early pace will likely be set by the Ethiopian trio (Haylom, Mesele, Berhe) or perhaps a pacemaker. The Australians thrive in sit-and-kick scenarios, but Haylom’s raw speed over the final 200m makes her the most dangerous closer. Expect a 2:05 first 800m, with the real surge coming at the bell.

**Athlete-by-Athlete Breakdown**

**1. Birke Haylom (ETH)** – *Predicted: 3:54.01*
At just 19, Haylom is the most improved middle-distance runner on the circuit. Her recent Shaoxing victory on 16 May 2026 (3:55.56) was a statement: she beat a loaded field that included Hull, Caldwell, and Ewoi. Haylom’s indoor season was superb, with a 4:00.62 in Ostrava and a 4:00.92 in Toruń. She possesses a devastating finishing kick (last 200m in ~28.5s in Shaoxing) and seems unfazed by senior competition. The only question mark is her age verification controversy, but on pure talent and recent form, she is the one to beat.

**2. Abbey Caldwell (AUS)** – *Predicted: 3:54.82*
Caldwell has matured into a world-class competitor. Her 3:56.12 at Shaoxing (3rd place) was her best-ever season opener, and she ran it with controlled aggression. She is the Oceanian record-holder in the 1000m, showing she has the speed to match Haylom. Caldwell’s 2025 season included a 3:59.32 in Rome and a 4:01.54 in Philadelphia, but her 2026 Australian summer was dominant (1:58.57 800m, 4:02.82 1500m in Perth). She thrives in championship-style races and will be hard to drop.

**3. Jessica Hull (AUS)** – *Predicted: 3:55.43*
Hull is the class of the field on paper—World bronze medallist in 2025, 3:52.67 performer at the Prefontaine Classic. However, her 2026 form has been erratic. She finished only 6th in Shaoxing (3:57.91) and had a disastrous 12th-place finish at the Australian Championships (4:32.96) in April. She also struggled at the World Indoor Championships (2nd in 3:59.45, but behind a slower tactical race). Hull is a 2000m world record-holder, so her endurance is unquestioned, but her sharpness over 1500m seems slightly off. She will run a smarter race than in Shaoxing and move up, but she lacks the edge of Haylom or Caldwell right now.

**4. Dorcus Ewoi (KEN)** – *Predicted: 3:55.71*
Ewoi was the surprise silver medallist at the 2025 World Championships (3:54.92), proving she can mix it with the best. She ran 3:57.74 in Shaoxing (5th), a solid if unspectacular result. Her indoor season was limited (4:01.22 in Boston), and her 2026 outdoor campaign has been low-key. Ewoi is a powerful 800m runner (1:57.15 at Worlds) who can sustain a hard pace, but she often fades slightly in the final 50m. She’ll be in the mix but likely just off the podium.

**5. Worknesh Mesele (ETH)** – *Predicted: 3:56.29*
Mesele is consistent but lacks a finishing gear. She ran 3:57.56 in Shaoxing (4th), just ahead of Ewoi. Her 2025 highlights include a 3:57.95 in Paris and a strong 800m leg at Worlds. She is disciplined and will not fall off the pace, but she rarely wins. Expect her to sit on the shoulder of the leaders and hold her position.

**6. Emily MacKay (USA)** – *Predicted: 3:56.88*
MacKay is the third-fastest American all-time in the 1500m and has a 3:57.91 from last year’s Prefontaine. She ran 3:58.54 in Shaoxing (7th) and looked comfortable, if not spectacular. Her 2026 indoor form was mixed (8:30.01 for 3000m at US Indoors, but only 4:14.25 in the 1500m final). She has the speed to run 3:55 but has not shown the consistency to challenge the top four here. She’s a solid top-six pick.

**7. Sarah Billings (AUS)** – *Predicted: 3:57.17*
Billings has quietly improved. She ran 3:58.81 in Shaoxing (8th), just behind MacKay, but has a 3:59.24 from the 2025 Rome Golden Gala. She is an Australian champion and has a strong 800m base (1:57.83). She’s not a pure 1500m specialist but is tough and will outfight some of the more fragile athletes behind her.

**8. Claudia Hollingsworth (AUS)** – *Predicted: 3:57.54*
At just 20, Hollingsworth is a rising star. She won the Australian 1500m title in April (4:17.06) and ran 3:58.84 in Shaoxing (9th). She also has a 3:58.09 from the Box Hill Classic in March. Her 800m times (1:57.67 at Silesia 2025) suggest she has the raw speed to run faster. However, her inexperience in high-stakes Diamond Leagues may cost her a few positions. She’s a future star but still learning.

**9. Linden Hall (AUS)** – *Predicted: 3:57.92*
At 34, Hall is the veteran of the field. She ran 3:58.96 in Shaoxing (10th) and has a 3:56.39 from Silesia 2025. Hall is an incredible competitor but her best days are behind her. She runs intelligent races and will likely benefit from a fast pace, but she no longer has the finishing speed to compete with the younger runners.

**10. Gracie Morris (USA)** – *Predicted: 3:58.45*
Morris had a strong indoor season (4:03.75 at World Indoors, 7th) but was only 12th in Shaoxing (4:00.29). She is more of a miler (4:23.74 PB) than a pure 1500m runner, and her 200%+ Olympic Trials performance may have taken a toll. She has the talent to be higher, but her recent results suggest she is a step behind the top Australians.

**11. Gabija Galvydytė (LTU)** – *Predicted: 3:58.91*
Galvydytė is a consistent mid-4:00 runner. She ran 3:59.74 in Shaoxing (11th) and has a 4:00.71 from Dublin 2025. She is a strong 800m runner (1:57.96 at Worlds) but lacks the endurance to hold on over 1500m against this depth. She will be in the second pack.

**12. Saron Berhe (ETH)** – *Predicted: 3:59.33*
Berhe is only 18 but has already run 3:57.72 at the Prefontaine Classic (2025). However, she struggled in Shaoxing (13th, 4:02.75) and has been inconsistent indoors. She is the U18 world record-holder over the mile, which speaks to her potential, but she is still developing tactically. Expect a mid-3:59 here.

**13. Revee Walcott-Nolan (GBR)** – *Predicted: 3:59.87*
Walcott-Nolan did not run the 1500m in Shaoxing (she DNF’d the 5000m), so her sharpness is uncertain. She has a 3:59.89 from Budapest 2025 and a strong indoor season (4:01.50 in Glasgow). She is a reliable British champion but not a regular sub-4:00 performer. She will be in the mix for the lower half of the top 10.

**14. Joceline Wind (SUI)** – *Predicted: 4:02.04*
Wind is a two-time Swiss champion and ran a solid 4:01.59 in Tomblaine (2025). However, she was 14th in Shaoxing (4:07.04) and has not shown the consistency to break 4:00. She is a classy runner but outmatched here.

**15. Chunhui Li (CHN)** – *Predicted: 4:05.38*
Li is the Asian 1500m champion and a strong domestic performer. However, her PB is only in the 4:06 range, and she was 15th in Shaoxing (4:11.67). Against world-class competition, she will struggle to hold the pace.

**16. Taryn Parks (USA)** – *Predicted: 4:08.10*
Parks is an NCAA-level runner who has not yet transitioned to the professional ranks effectively. She DNF’d in Shaoxing, suggesting she was out of her depth. Her best 1500m times are around 4:09, and she will likely be the first to be gapped.

**Final Summary**

The race will likely come down to Haylom and Caldwell, with Hull hanging on for third. Haylom’s youth, confidence, and recent victory give her the edge. Caldwell is the safer pick for a podium, but Hull’s pedigree means she cannot be counted out. The Australian contingent (Caldwell, Hull, Billings, Hollingsworth, Hall) will look to control the race tactically, but Haylom’s explosive kick may prove decisive. Ewoi and Mesele will push the pace but do not have the raw speed to win. Expect a fast, honest race with multiple women dipping under 3:56.

### Race Preview & Reasoning

The Xiamen Diamond League on 23 May 2026 brings together a deep field of nine hurdlers, headlined by the “big three” of the event over the past decade: world‑record holder **Karsten Warholm** (29), 2022 world champion **Alison dos Santos** (25), and Asian record‑holder **Abderrahman Samba** (30). However, the most telling recent form comes from the 300 m hurdles race in Shaoxing just one week earlier (16 May 2026). There, **dos Santos** edged **Warholm** 33.01 to 33.05, while rising star **Matheus Lima** (22) clocked 33.75. That race is the closest analogue to 400 m hurdle rhythm and endurance, and it strongly suggests dos Santos has the sharpest speed‑endurance right now.

**1. Alison dos Santos** – The Brazilian is on a remarkable run. His 33.01 in Shaoxing is a world‑class 300 m hurdles time, and he has been posting blistering flat 400 m times (44.38 in April 2026) and a 21.85 in the rare 200 m hurdles. He also won the 2025 Stockholm Diamond League (46.68) and finished 2nd at the 2025 World Championships (46.84). His turnover and confidence at the barriers are at an all‑time high. Expect him to dictate the race from gun to tape, winning in **47.22** – similar to his 46.84 World final but on a slightly slower early‑season track.

**2. Karsten Warholm** – The Norwegian legend remains a threat, but his 2025 season had clear wobbles: he was only 5th at the Tokyo World Championships (47.58) and lost to dos Santos in Stockholm (47.41 vs 46.68). His 33.05 in Shaoxing shows he’s still elite, but he hasn’t recaptured his 46.28 Silesia form from August 2025. Warholm’s trademark aggressive start and powerful finish will keep him in contention, but dos Santos’s superior recent flat speed gives him the edge. Prediction: **47.38**.

**3. Matheus Lima** – The 22‑year‑old Brazilian is the breakout of 2025–26. He ran 33.75 in the 300 m hurdles (only 0.70 behind the top two), won the South American indoor 400 m title (45.85), and clocked 48.08 over hurdles in Shanghai 2025. At the World Championships he reached the semi‑final (48.16) and has since improved his flat 400 m to 44.90. He is fearless and technically sound. In Xiamen, he will challenge Samba for third and could even push for second if Warholm falters. **47.55** is a realistic step forward.

**4. Abderrahman Samba** – The Qatari is the most experienced after Warholm and dos Santos, but his recent results are patchy. He won bronze at the 2025 Worlds (47.06) and ran 47.34 in Silesia, but his 16 May 2026 outing over 400 m hurdles was a sluggish 48.85 in Doha. That is nearly a second slower than his peak. Samba has often struggled to maintain early‑season form and may need more races to sharpen. Expect a middle‑pack battle, but his pedigree earns him **47.68**.

**5. Trevor Bassitt** – The American is a consistent sub‑48 performer. He ran 47.82 in April 2026 at Tom Jones Memorial and 48.14 in Paris 2025. His 300 m hurdles time of 34.02 in Shaoxing is solid and shows he can handle the early pace. Bassitt lacks the top‑end gear of the podium contenders but is reliable for a mid‑47. **47.85** matches his recent arc.

**6. Caleb Dean** – The 24‑year‑old NCAA champion made the World final in 2025 (7th, 48.20) and has shown flashes of brilliance (47.76 at US Championships). However, his 34.51 in the 300 m hurdles was only 6th, and his flat 400 m times (45.18) are behind the leaders. He is still developing and may struggle to hold the closing stages. **47.98** is a fair estimate.

**7. CJ Allen** – The 30‑year‑old American is a steady performer (48.00 in Zurich 2025, NACAC champion) but his 34.53 in the 300 m hurdles indicates he is slightly off his best. He lacks the raw speed to challenge the top five. **48.15** reflects his consistent but non‑elite level.

He finished 9th in the Shaoxing 300 m hurdles (35.72) and was well off 49‑seconds in his 2025 races. He also DNS’d a flat 400 m in April. McMaster appears either injured or out of shape. A time near **48.65** would be a minor victory.

**Conclusion:** Alison dos Santos enters as the man to beat, backed by the fastest 300 m hurdle time of the year and a string of dominant flat‑speed performances. Warholm will fight hard but may have to settle for second again, while the young Matheus Lima announces himself as the next big star by claiming bronze ahead of a fading Samba.

1. Ferdinand Omanyala (KEN) – **9.93**

### Race Preview & Reasoning

The Xiamen Diamond League on 23 May 2026 arrives just one week after the Shaoxing Diamond League (16 May), where many of these athletes raced. That result provides a clear, recent form guide. The conditions in Xiamen are typically warm and often wind-neutral, favouring clean times. Here’s how the field shapes up:

**1. Ferdinand Omanyala (30)**  
Omanyala is the form man of the pack. He has been consistently sub-10 throughout 2026, winning the Kip Keino Classic (9.96) and the Botswana Golden Grand Prix (9.95) before placing 2nd in Shaoxing with 9.98. At 30, he remains the African record holder (9.77) and has shown no signs of slowing. His explosive start and powerful drive phase give him a slight edge over the rest, especially after a week’s rest. Expect him to dip just under 9.95.

**2. Kenneth Bednarek (27)**  
Bednarek is a proven championship performer (US champion in 2025 with 9.79 legal). In 2026, he ran a solid 9.98 at Shaoxing, but that was only 3rd. He tends to run faster in bigger races; his 2025 season included 9.86 in Philadelphia and 9.79 at US Champs. At 27, he’s in his prime. The key is his start – if he can stay close to Omanyala early, his finishing speed is elite. A 9.94 is well within his range, and he may challenge for the win if the race is clean.

**3. Gift Leotlela (27)**  
The South African sprinter is the surprise winner of Shaoxing with 9.97, a lifetime best-legal. He has been steady all spring, winning the South African title (10.15 in windy conditions) and placing well in Europe. He ran 9.95 (wind-aided) in 2025 but has now delivered a genuine 9.97. Leotlela’s top-end speed is excellent, but he lacks the raw power of Omanyala or Bednarek. He should repeat a low-9.9 performance, but the top two have a higher ceiling.

**4. Trayvon Bromell (30)**  
Bromell is a veteran and former world indoor champion (2026 bronze in 60m with 6.45). His outdoor 2026 started with a 10.06 in College Station, then 10.01 at Shaoxing. That’s a slight improvement. He has run 9.84 in 2025 but has been inconsistent in finals (4th at US Champs, 6th in Zurich). At 30, he is still quick but no longer a sub-9.8 threat. A 9.97 would be a solid return, but he may struggle to hold off the younger, faster men.

**5. Lachlan Kennedy (22)**  
The Australian prodigy broke the 10-second barrier on home soil in 2026, winning the national title in 9.96. He backed that up with 10.01 at Shaoxing, placing 5th. Kennedy is still learning to race at the Diamond League level, but his 60m pedigree (world indoor silver) shows he has elite speed. He tends to fade slightly in the closing metres compared to more experienced sprinters. A 9.99 would match his best legal time and put him in the mix for a top-5 finish.

**6. Akani Simbine (32)**  
The 32-year-old South African has been a perennial finalist but has never quite broken through for a major medal. His 2026 season is modest: 10.05 at Shaoxing, 10.05 in London 2025. He ran 9.82 (African record) in Paris 2024 but hasn’t matched that since. Simbine is reliable and rarely runs worse than 10.05, but he lacks the speed to dip under 10.0 consistently at this stage. A 10.02 is a fair estimate.

**7. Letsile Tebogo (22)**  
Tebogo is primarily a 200m/400m specialist (Olympic 200m champion). In 2026, he has run only a few 100m races, with a best of 10.12 in Shaoxing (7th). His 100m performances are often experimental, and he often focuses on the longer sprints. He has raw talent but is not in peak 100m shape. 10.07 is a reasonable prediction, but he could surprise if he decides to go all out.

**8. Christian Coleman (29)**  
The former world champion and 60m WR holder (6.34) has struggled in 2026. His Shaoxing race (10.19, 8th) was well off his best. He had a solid 2025 (9.86 at US Champs, 9.97 win in Zurich) but has not carried that into 2026. At 29, questions about his form and consistency linger. A 10.10 would be a minor improvement, but he is clearly not in the same league as the leaders right now.

**9. Xinrui Deng (22)**  
The Chinese youngster is the reigning national champion and a sub-10.10 runner (10.06 in 2025). However, his 2026 outdoor races have been slower (10.23–10.28) and he is untested against this calibre of international field. A 10.16 would be a solid showing for him, but he is unlikely to challenge for points.

**10. Shengjie Wang (25)**  
Wang is primarily a relay runner (4x100m) and has not broken 10.15 in the 100m. His best in 2025 was 10.15, and he has no 2026 individual race listed better than 10.22 (inferred from relay splits). He is likely to anchor the Chinese relay but is outclassed here. A 10.22 is optimistic.

**Overall Summary**  
The race will be a battle between Omanyala and Bednarek, with Leotlela and Bromell in the next tier. Kennedy is the young wildcard, while the veterans Simbine, Tebogo, and Coleman are struggling to keep pace. The Xiamen crowd will roar for the Chinese duo, but the podium will be decided by the African and American speedsters. Expect a close, fast race with the winning time in the 9.93–9.94 range.

### Preview & Prediction Analysis

This field is a fascinating mix of generational talent, championship pedigree, and emerging speedsters. The key to the prediction lies in the *trends* shown in the early 2026 season, specifically the recent Shaoxing Diamond League on 16 May 2026, which acts as the most direct form guide for this Xiamen race. The results there are the clearest indicator of who is carrying momentum into this meet.

**The Battle for the Title: Russell vs. Charlton**

The top two positions appear to be a two-woman race. **Masai Russell** enters as the clear favourite. At just 25, she is the reigning Olympic champion and American record holder (12.17). Critically, she has already raced on Chinese soil this season, winning the Shaoxing Diamond League on 16 May with a commanding **12.25**. That wasn't a one-off; she ran 12.40 (+0.5) and 12.47 (+1.2) in the lead-up to that win. Her season is perfectly programmed for a peak in late May, and her ability to execute under pressure – a trait honed by her Olympic gold – makes her the most reliable performer in this field. She is fastest to the first hurdle and has the best top-end speed of the group.

**Devynne Charlton** is the most dangerous challenger. The 30-year-old Bahamian is the world record holder in the 60m hurdles (7.65, set at the 2026 World Indoor Championships in March). That indoor campaign was dominant: she won every major final she entered, culminating in a historic WR. Her transition to the outdoor season has been seamless. She finished 2nd in Shaoxing with a very sharp **12.38** (+0.4), directly behind Russell. Her form is superb. She may lack Russell’s raw flat speed at the end of the race, but her technical precision and consistent rhythm make her a near-certainty for the podium and a real threat for the win if Russell has a slight misstep. She will push Russell all the way.

**The Contenders and the Wild Cards: Nugent, Kambundji, Amusan**

**Ackera Nugent** is the wild card of the field. The 23-year-old Jamaican has the second-fastest PB in the field (12.30) and looked incredible in the summer of 2025, consistently running 12.3s. However, her start to 2026 has been puzzlingly poor. She finished a distant 6th in Shaoxing with **12.98** and ran only 11.52 in a flat 100m recently. This suggests she may be working through an injury or a technical rebuild. Her talent is undeniable—she’s a former World U20 champion and ran 12.30 in the 2025 Diamond League Final. If she is right, she is a podium threat. But based on recent evidence, she is a significant risk. I predict a partial bounce-back to 12.35, which would be a strong performance, but it won't be enough to beat the Russell/Charlton duo in their current form.

**Ditaji Kambundji** is the reigning World Champion (Tokyo 2025, 12.24). That is a massive credential. However, her 2026 outdoor season has started slowly. She was 5th in Shaoxing with **12.82**. While her indoor season was solid (placing 2nd at World Indoors with a 7.75 PB in the final), she hasn't yet translated that into outdoor speed. The lack of early-season races between 12.4 and 12.5 is a concern. She is a brilliant championship performer who will peak for the European Championships and the Diamond League Final, but on 23 May, she is likely still building towards that level.

**Tobi Amusan** is the most intriguing entry. The world record holder is now 28. Her 2025 was a step down from her 2022-2023 peak, finishing 2nd at the World Championships. Her 2026 season has been inconsistent. She won the African Championships but in modest times (12.84). She was 3rd in Shaoxing with **12.41**, which is her best result of the year. That shows she is still capable of running fast. However, she has not run under 12.30 in a legal wind since 2023. Her once-unassailable speed seems a fraction lower. She is a brilliant technician and will be a threat for 4th, but the raw speed of Russell and the consistency of Charlton look too much to overcome. She is vulnerable to a fully-fit Nugent or a sharp Kambundji.

**The Veterans and the Home Athletes: Simmonds, Williams, Marshall, Wu, Liu**

**Tonea Marshall** (USA) and **Megan Simmonds** (JAM) are solid, experienced performers. Marshall ran a wind-aided 12.24 in 2025 but has had a quiet 2026, including a DNF in Shaoxing. Simmonds is consistent in the 12.6-12.7 range and ran 12.73 in Shaoxing. They are class athletes but lack the top-end speed of the leaders.
**Danielle Williams**, the wily 33-year-old two-time world champion, is the ultimate tactician. However, she also DNF'd in Shaoxing, and her flat 100m form this year suggests her top speed is waning. She will be competitive but won't challenge for the win.
**Yanni Wu** and **Jingyang Liu** are the local heroes. Wu is the more established of the two, with a PB of 12.76. Liu recently ran a PB of 12.81 in November 2025. They will be roared on by the home crowd, which could lift them to season’s bests. However, they operate in a different time zone to the top internationals. A time around 13.0-13.1 represents a very good day at the office, placing them in the bottom two spots.

**Conclusion:**

This is Masai Russell's race to lose. Her victory in Shaoxing a week prior, combined with her consistent early-season speed, makes her the undeniable favourite. Devynne Charlton, riding the high of her World Indoor record and her own strong run in Shaoxing, is the clear second pick. The battle for third is a fascinating toss-up between the struggling but talented Ackera Nugent, the building World Champion Ditaji Kambundji, and the legendary Tobi Amusan. Based solely on the most recent performance data (Shaoxing), Nugent is a major risk, and Kambundji hasn't yet shown her best. Therefore, the edge for third goes to Nugent on raw talent alone, with Kambundji and Amusan duelling closely behind. Expect a high-quality race with times reflecting the early-season conditions and a powerful head-to-head duel between the new American star and the Bahamian record-breaker.

blurbs.Discus Women:
**Predicted Finish and Marks for Women's Discus Throw – Rabat Diamond League (31 May 2026)**  

1. **Valarie Sion (USA)** – 68.75 m  
2. **Jorinde van Klinken (NED)** – 67.30 m  
3. **Laulauga Tausaga (USA)** – 66.45 m  
4. **Jayden Ulrich (USA)** – 66.10 m  
5. **Shanice Craft (GER)** – 65.85 m  
6. **Cierra Jackson (USA)** – 65.60 m  
7. **Bin Feng (CHN)** – 65.40 m  
8. **Marike Steinacker (GER)** – 65.05 m  
9. **Erika Beistle (USA)** – 64.60 m  
10. **Vanessa Kamga (SWE)** – 64.20 m  
11. **Liliana Cá (POR)** – 62.80 m  

---

### Reasoning and Analysis  

#### 1. Valarie Sion – The Undisputed Favorite  
Sion enters Rabat as the reigning Olympic and World champion, with a career defined by consistency at the highest level. Her 2025 season featured six Diamond League wins and a World gold (69.48 m). In 2026, she has already thrown 73.10 m (Oklahoma Throws Series, April) and 68.45 m to win the Xiamen Diamond League on 23 May – just one week before Rabat. That recent 68.45 m is a clear statement of form, and her ability to produce 68–70 m in competition is unmatched. Even a rare 6th-place finish (65.18 m) in early April was an anomaly; she rebounded immediately with 73.10 m. Sion’s North American record (73.52 m) and her head-to-head dominance over every rival in this field – she beat van Klinken at the 2025 World Championships (69.48 vs. 67.50) and has never lost to Tausaga or Ulrich in a Diamond League – make her a lock for the win. Expect a composed series around 68.75 m, possibly higher if conditions are favorable.

#### 2. Jorinde van Klinken – High Ceiling, Recent Dip  
Van Klinken owns the Dutch record (70.99 m, set in April 2026 at Oklahoma) and is the only athlete other than Sion to have cleared 70 m this season. However, her Xiamen performance (64.27 m, 3rd) was a significant drop, suggesting she may still be adjusting between shot put and discus. Despite that, her 2025 season was remarkably solid: she placed 2nd at Worlds (67.50 m) and was runner-up in multiple Diamond League meets (Paris, Zürich). Her 70.99 m shows she can peak, and Rabat likely offers a better environment than the long travel to China. Van Klinken tends to bounce back after a poor outing – after a 4th at Xiamen in 2025 (64.79 m), she threw 66.22 m the following week. Here, she should return to the 67 m range, finishing clear of the chasing pack.

#### 3. Laulauga Tausaga – Former Champion Seeking Consistency  
Tausaga is a 2023 World champion with a 2025 personal best of 70.72 m (2nd at Oklahoma), but her 2026 season has been erratic. After a promising 62.87 m in early May, she managed only 61.51 m at Xiamen (8th), her worst Diamond League result in years. This inconsistency – she also finished 6th at the 2025 World Championships (65.49 m) – stems from technical issues under pressure. Yet her peak is undeniable; she threw 70.72 m in a head-to-head with Sion’s 73.52 m in 2025. In Rabat, away from the long-haul travel that may have affected Xiamen, and with a week to refocus, Tausaga should improve to the mid-66 m range. She has historically outperformed Ulrich and Craft when dialed in, as shown by her 64.94 m at the 2025 Prefontaine Classic, where she beat both.

#### 4. Jayden Ulrich – Rising Star with Momentum  
At 23, Ulrich is the youngest of the top Americans and has shown clear progression. Her 2026 season includes a 65.49 m at the Oklahoma Throws Series (5th) and a 65.08 m win at the USATF Throws Festival on 23 May – the same day as Xiamen. That mark is just 0.37 m shy of her personal best (65.49 m), indicating strong recent form. She also threw 65.39 m at Oklahoma in April. Ulrich’s NCAA title in 2025 (65.82 m) and her 2nd-place finish at the 2024 Olympic Trials prove she rises to the occasion. While she has never beaten van Klinken or Tausaga in a Diamond League, her consistency in the 65 m range surpasses Craft and Jackson this spring. Rabat will be her first DL of the year outside the US, but her trajectory suggests a breakthrough near 66 m, enough for 4th.

#### 5. Shanice Craft – Solid German Veteran  
Craft, 32, is a three-time European bronze medalist and a model of consistency. Her 2026 best is 66.03 m (Magdeburg, May 14), and she followed with 65.21 m the next weekend. At Xiamen she slipped to 63.96 m (6th), but that was her first outing of the year outside Europe. Craft’s 2025 season included a 68.10 m win in Wiesbaden and a 65.21 m at Worlds (8th). She rarely throws below 64 m and is reliable in big meets. Her style – smooth, rhythmic – suits the Rabat venue. Expect a rebound to the mid-65 m range, placing her ahead of the more volatile Jackson and Feng.

#### 6. Cierra Jackson – Talented but Inconsistent  
Jackson stunned the field with a 67.82 m at the 2025 Prefontaine Classic (2nd) and won the NCAA title (65.82 m). In 2026, she threw 67.25 m at Oklahoma (4th) but managed only 62.66 m at Xiamen (7th). That inconsistency mirrors her 2025 season, where she followed a 67.82 m with a 58.33 m at US Championships. At just 23, she still lacks the steadiness of the top group. However, her ceiling is high, and in a multi‑round competition she can produce a big throw. If she channels her Prefontaine form, she could challenge Craft. Given her recent 62–63 m trend, a 65.60 m is realistic – enough for 6th, but vulnerable to a poor round.

#### 7. Bin Feng – The Steady Chinese Thrower  
Feng, 31, was Olympic silver medalist in 2024 and World champion in 2022. She is less flashy than the Americans but extremely reliable in the 64–65 m range. At Xiamen on 23 May, she threw 65.03 m for 2nd place, her best of 2026. That performance came after a 63.28 m in May, showing upward trend. Her 2025 season included a 65.52 m at Worlds (7th) and consistent 64+ m in DL meets. Feng thrives in Asian conditions, but Rabat may be a step up in competition. She typically struggles against the depth of the US and European throwers – she was 5th at Xiamen 2025 (64.17 m) and 6th at Golden Gala (64.19 m). She should maintain her 65 m level but lacks the extra gear to overtake Jackson or Craft when they hit their marks.

#### 8. Marike Steinacker – Solid but Declining Form  
Steinacker, 33, placed 4th at the 2024 Olympics and is a perennial German champion. Her 2026 season opened with a 66.55 m (Oklahoma, April) and a 65.54 m in Magdeburg (May 14). However, her most recent results show a slight drop: 64.20 m in Wiesbaden (May 22) and 62.63 m in Rehlingen (May 24). That trend, plus a neutral‑warm‑up meet in Europe a week before Rabat, suggests she may be slightly fatigued. At Xiamen she did not compete, so she is fresh, but her peak is likely 65 m. She has been consistently behind Craft this season (Craft beat her in Magdeburg and Halle). Expect 65.05 m, just behind Feng.

#### 9. Erika Beistle – Impressive but Untested at This Level  
Beistle, 22, is a NCAA Division II standout who has rapidly improved. Her 2026 best is 66.72 m (May 10), and she threw 64.07 m at Xiamen (4th) – a remarkable result for someone with limited DL experience. That Xiamen mark was her first international Diamond League, and she handled it well. However, her consistency is questionable: she followed the 66.72 m with a 64.07 m, and earlier in the season she had a 64.54 m at Oklahoma. In a field with several proven 65+ m throwers, she may struggle to repeat that level under the pressure of a stronger lineup. Rabat will be her second DL, and the step up in opposition could lead to a slightly lower mark around 64.60 m, placing her 9th.

#### 10. Vanessa Kamga – Consistent but Lower Ceiling  
Kamga, 27, set her personal best (66.61 m) in the 2025 World final (4th). This season, she has been hovering around 64 m: 64.02 m at Xiamen (5th), 64.00 m in Varberg, and 64.22 m in 2025. She is a solid competitor but lacks the explosive marks of those above her. Her 2026 European Throwing Cup result (58.82 m) was poor, but she rebounded in Xiamen. She tends to produce mid‑64 m throws in non‑peak meets, and with no recent 65+ m, she falls behind the 65‑m group. Rabat will likely see her at 64.20 m, a typical result for her.

#### 11. Liliana Cá – Age and Form Decline  
Cá, 39, is past her prime. Her 2026 best is 61.89 m (European Champions Cup, May 23), and she has not thrown 65 m since 2023. Her 2025 season included a 65.35 m in Lisbon, but she was only 9th at Worlds (59.79 m). She has been a consistent 62–63 m thrower this spring, but that level is 2–3 meters behind the rest of the field. In a Diamond League with strong depth, she will struggle to break 63 m. Her experience may help in execution, but the physical decline is evident. 62.80 m is a fair estimate for 11th.

### Summary  
Sion’s dominance is unquestioned, while van Klinken and Tausaga possess the highest peaks. Ulrich and Craft offer reliable 65‑m consistency, and Jackson, Feng, and Steinacker fill the next tier. Beistle and Kamga are capable but not yet at the same level, and Cá rounds out the field. The Rabat meeting, typically held in warm conditions with a fast ring, should reward athletes who can maintain technique under pressure – an area where Sion, van Klinken, and Craft excel.

3. **Angelina Topić (SRB)** – 1.97 m  
4. **Maria Żodzik (POL)** – 1.95 m  
5. **Eleanor Patterson (AUS)** – 1.94 m  
6. **Vashti Cunningham (USA)** – 1.93 m  
7. **Morgan Lake (GBR)** – 1.92 m  
8. **Lamara Distin (JAM)** – 1.91 m  
9. **Charity Hufnagel (USA)** – 1.90 m  
10. **Imke Onnen (GER)** – 1.88 m  

---

### Preview & Reasoning

**1. Yaroslava Mahuchikh**  
Mahuchikh enters Rabat as the overwhelming favourite. At 24, she is the world record holder (2.10 m) and has proven she can produce big results on the Diamond League circuit. Her 2026 indoor campaign was peerless: she cleared 2.03 m in Lviv in January, 2.01 m at the World Indoor Championships in Toruń (where she won gold), and she went undefeated indoors. Outdoors in 2025, she consistently cleared 2.00 m or better (Xiamen, Doha, Chorzów, Zürich). Even her rare off-days (a no-height in Lausanne, a 4th in London) are outliers. The only concern is her "World Championships hangover" – she took bronze in Tokyo 2025, but that was in a brutally deep field. In Rabat, she will dictate the bar progression and likely attempt 2.02–2.04 m, but a clean 2.00 m on first attempt should be enough to win. She is simply the most technically polished and clutch jumper in the field.

**2. Yuliia Levchenko**  
Levchenko has been on a quiet resurgence. At 28, she is still improving – she jumped 2.00 m in Zürich in August 2025 (her second-best outdoor mark ever) and won silver at the 2026 World Indoor Championships with 1.99 m. Crucially, she has just come off a victory at the Xiamen Diamond League on 23 May 2026, where she cleared 1.99 m, beating Mahuchikh (who did not compete). That win, combined with her consistent 1.95–1.99 m range indoors and outdoors, positions her as the clear #2. She lacks Mahuchikh’s ceiling but is more reliable than the rest of the field. Her one weakness is that she sometimes struggles in crowded competitions (11th in Paris 2025), but Rabat’s smaller field should suit her.

**3. Angelina Topić**  
The 20-year-old Serbian star is the most exciting young jumper in the world. She won silver at the 2026 World Indoor Championships (1.99 m) and has already set the Serbian outdoor record at 2.00 m. In 2025, she medalled at the World Championships (bronze, 1.97 m) and won the European U23 title. Her indoor 2.00 m in Banská Bystrica in February 2026 was a statement. However, she is still learning to handle back-to-back high-level outdoor meets – she was 8th in Stockholm and 7th in Paris during the 2025 Diamond League season. The step up to a consistent 1.98–2.00 m outdoors will come, but Rabat may be just short of a win. She could push Levchenko for second, but Levchenko’s recent 1.99 m win gives her the edge.

**4. Maria Żodzik**  
Żodzik, now 28 and representing Poland, has developed into a consistent 1.95–2.00 m jumper. She was silver medallist at the 2025 World Championships (2.00 m) and won the Polish indoor title in 2026. Her indoor season was strong (1.98 m in Toruń), but her outdoor diamond league returns have been more moderate (4th in Xiamen in 2026). She tends to peak for championships, not necessarily for early-season Diamond Leagues. In Rabat, she should clear 1.95 m, but she may lack the sharpness to challenge the top three. A 1.95 m is a solid floor, but she has not shown the ability to go 1.98 m+ in a non-championship setting recently.

**5. Eleanor Patterson**  
The 2022 World Champion, now 29, has been a model of consistency but has dipped slightly from her peak 2022–2023 form. She cleared 1.97 m indoors in 2025 (silver at World Indoors) and outdoors in 2025 (Australian Championships, Paris). However, her 2026 season has been more muted: she jumped 1.93 m at Australian Champs and 1.94 m in Xiamen (5th). She is still a threat on her day – her technique is superb – but she seems to lack the extra gear to reach 1.98 m+ right now. She will likely settle into a 1.94 m battle with Cunningham, and her cleaner form should give her the edge.

**6. Vashti Cunningham**  
Cunningham, 27, is a two-time world indoor champion (2022, 2026) and a proven competitor, but she has struggled to translate that indoor dominance to consistent outdoor results. In 2025, she was 10th at World Indoors and 10th at World Championships outdoors. Her 2026 indoor season was better (2nd US Indoors, 1.96 m), but her outdoor opener in Xiamen was only 1.91 m (6th). She has the talent to beat 1.97 m (USA Champs 2025), but she often fails to deliver in the biggest outdoor fields. Rabat’s strong line-up may see her settle at 1.93 m, a mark she can clear, but not enough to climb higher.

**7. Morgan Lake**  
Lake, 28, is the British record holder (2.00 m) and had a brilliant 2025 season, including a 2.00 m win in Zürich. However, her 2026 form has been inconsistent: she was 8th in Xiamen (1.88 m) and did not medal at World Indoors (5th in 2025, no final in 2026). She seems to be struggling to find her rhythm outdoors. Her best diamond league finishes in 2025 were 1st in London (1.96 m) and 3rd in Zürich, but that was against weaker fields. In this deep lineup, she will need to jump 1.94 m+ to break the top five, but her recent results suggest she is closer to 1.90–1.92 m. A 1.92 m is a reasonable prediction.

**8. Lamara Distin**  
Distin, the Jamaican record holder (1.97 m), has shown flashes but has not consistently challenged the world’s best. She jumped 1.96 m indoors in February 2026 and 1.94 m in Xiamen, but she was 10th at World Indoors outdoors in 2025 (no-height). She is capable of 1.94 m on a good day, but she often struggles to maintain that level in high-pressure diamond league settings. Her 1.94 m in Xiamen is a promising sign, but the competition in Rabat is stronger than in Xiamen. She may be relegated to 1.91 m.

**9. Charity Hufnagel**  
Hufnagel, 24, is the reigning US indoor champion (1.96 m in 2026) and had a strong indoor tour, but her outdoor form has been unspectacular. She jumped 1.91 m in Xiamen (6th) and 1.84 m at Penn Relays. She has yet to prove she can transfer her indoor success to the outdoor circuit, where the wind and approach conditions change. She is a solid 1.90 m jumper, but in this field, that will slot her near the back. Her ceiling is 1.94 m, but she has not shown it outdoors recently.

**10. Imke Onnen**  
Onnen, now 31, is a seasoned veteran but has never broken through to the elite echelon. Her personal best is 1.94 m outdoors, and she has jumped only 1.91 m in 2026 (indoor German title). She was 8th at World Indoors (1.89 m) and 9th in Xiamen (1.88 m). The field is simply too strong for her to compete for top-five finishes. She will likely start at 1.85 m and fail at 1.91 m, settling for 1.88 m. A respectable effort for an athlete past her prime.

### Key factors for the order:
- **Form from Xiamen (23 May 2026)**: Levchenko’s 1.99 m win, Distin’s 1.94 m (3rd), and Patterson’s 1.94 m (5th) all factor directly into Rabat predictions.
- **Head-to-head history**: Mahuchikh has beaten every athlete here multiple times in 2025/2026. Levchenko has beaten Topić in recent indoor/outdoor meets.
- **Age and trend**: Topić (20) is still rising; Onnen (31) is declining. Levchenko (28) is at her peak; Cunningham (27) has plateaued.
- **Indoor-to-outdoor translation**: Hufnagel, Lake, and Cunningham have stronger indoor profiles than outdoor, while Mahuchikh, Levchenko, and Topić are equally good in both.

Rabat’s meet is early in the outdoor season, so athletes will not yet be at their absolute PBs. Expect solid, clean jumps rather than record attempts. Mahuchikh will control the bar, Levchenko will push her, and Topić will announce herself as a genuine contender for the Diamond League title.

Given his upward trajectory and confidence, a slight improvement to 22.41 m is realistic.

His Xiamen mark of 21.41 m (3rd) was well below his standard, and his only 22+ meter effort in 2026 came at the World Championships last September. While he often finds another gear in championship-style meetings, Rabat is a Diamond League stop, and his recent form suggests he won’t reach 22.30+ just yet. A rebound to 22.17 m is plausible given his pedigree, but Campbell’s momentum gives him the edge.

**3. Jordan Geist** has been quietly rising. He took 2nd in Xiamen with 21.52 m, a solid outdoor opener, and his indoor 2026 was outstanding: 22.04 m wins in Ostrava and Madrid, plus a silver at the World Indoor Championships (21.64 m). At 27, he is improving rapidly and appears more consistent than the veterans below. His 21.89 m prediction reflects a step up from Xiamen as he gains confidence on the Diamond League circuit.

His 2026 indoor season peaked at 21.92 m, and he finished 5th at the US Indoor Championships (20.18 m). His last truly dominant outdoor performance was in 2025 (22.48 m in Eugene), but that was a year ago. Without a recent Diamond League outing, he is hard to place above the younger, more active competitors. A 21.68 m return is respectful of his talent but acknowledges his reduced sharpness.

**6. Leonardo Fabbri** had a superb 2025 (Italian record 22.82 m) but has been erratic. He recorded a no-mark in Xiamen, which could indicate a technical issue or a foul-heavy competition. Earlier in May he threw 21.88 m in Savona, suggesting his fitness is solid. At 29, he should be in his prime, but the inconsistency (12th at 2025 European Indoors, 7th at 2026 World Indoors) drops him below the more reliable performers. A 21.62 m is a recovery mark.

**7. Payton Otterdahl** is a strong thrower (22.35 m at 2025 US Championships) but did not compete in Xiamen, making his current form uncertain. His 2026 season lacks a major outdoor result so far; his last listed mark is a 21.81 m win at a small meet in April. He tends to perform best in US-based meets, and Rabat may not bring out his peak. A 21.55 m is a reasonable guess, but he could be higher if he finds rhythm.

**8. Roger Steen** at 34 is a reliable 21-meter thrower, as shown by his 4th place in Xiamen (21.25 m) and his consistent indoor season (21.88 m in Madrid, 21.81 m US indoor champion). **9. Adrian Piperi** struggled in Xiamen (20.57 m, 7th) and has not thrown over 22 m in 2026. At 27, he has promise but appears to be in a slump after a solid 2025 (22.29 m at US Championships). With no recent standout to suggest a turnaround, a 20.92 m prediction is respectful of his ability but reflects his current difficulties.

**Predicted Finish and Marks for the Women’s Pole Vault – Rabat Diamond League, 31 May 2026**

1. Katie Moon (USA) – **4.81 m**  
2. Molly Caudery (GBR) – **4.78 m**  
3. Tina Šutej (SLO) – **4.75 m**

---

### Why This Order?

**Katie Moon** enters Rabat as the defending champion (won here in 2025 with 4.73 m) and the 2025 World champion (4.90 m). Her 2026 season has been methodical: a comfortable 4.75 m at the Drake Relays (20 April) and a 4.60 m win at High Point (17 May) suggest she is rounding into form without peaking too early. Her indoor campaign (4.70 m in Liévin) was solid, and her consistency over the past two years—including five Diamond League wins in 2025—makes her the clear favourite. Expect her to clear 4.81 m, matching her typical early-summer output.

**Molly Caudery** is the reigning World Indoor champion (2026, 4.85 m) and holds the British record of 4.92 m. Her outdoor opener on 17 May was a modest 4.61 m, but she has a history of building through the season. Her indoor mark in Toruń (4.85 m) is the highest any athlete has jumped so far in 2026, and she thrives on the big stage. At 25, she has the youthful explosiveness to challenge Moon, but her relative lack of outdoor reps in 2026 may leave her a few centimetres short. A 4.78 m clearance would be a strong statement.

**Tina Šutej** (37 years old) is defying age with a superlative indoor season: 4.80 m in Metz and again at the World Indoor Championships (silver). She also won the 2025 World Championships bronze (4.80 m) and was second in Rabat last year (4.63 m). Her outdoor transition can sometimes be slightly slower, but her technique is rock-solid. She will likely match or exceed her 2025 Rabat mark, hitting 4.75 m. Her veteran savvy could push her higher if the leaders struggle.

**Sandi Morris** (33) remains a perennial contender, but her 2026 outdoor form has been erratic. She cleared 4.75 m at the Drake Relays indoor-style vault, but then slipped to 4.65 m and 4.55 m in subsequent meets. Her 2025 season included a 4.85 m at the US Championships and a 4.85 m silver at Worlds, so the ability is there. However, the slight dip in consistency—especially a 4.54 m at the 2025 Memorial Van Damme—suggests she may not be at her absolute peak in late May. A 4.72 m jump is a realistic ceiling, placing her fourth.

**Imogen Ayris** has been on a sharp upward trajectory. She won the 2026 World Indoor bronze (4.70 m), and just one week before Rabat, on 23 May, she cleared 4.70 m in Kifisia. That recent outdoors victory shows she carries excellent form. Her indoor All Star Perche result (4.76 m in February) indicates she is capable of even higher. Ayris is a strong bet for 4.70 m and could surprise if the top four falter.

**Angelica Moser** (28) is a consistent 4.70+ jumper but has not yet competed outdoors in 2026. Her indoor season peaked with a 4.70 m at the World Indoors (3rd) and a 4.76 m in Clermont-Ferrand. However, she has a history of slightly lower outdoor marks early in the summer—her 2025 Rabat result was only 4.50 m. Until she proves she can replicate her indoor heights on the outdoor runway, 4.66 m is a fair prediction.

**Nina Kennedy** (28) is the Olympic gold medallist (2024) and World co-champion (2023), but her 2026 campaign has been limited. She jumped 4.72 m in Melbourne (28 March) and 4.65 m at the Australian Championships (11 April), but she has not competed internationally since. The travel and lack of recent high-level competition in a deep field may affect her rhythm. She is capable of 4.80+ on a good day, but given her sparse schedule, a 4.62 m opener is more likely.

**Olivia McTaggart** (25) has shown flashes of brilliance—4.73 m at the 2025 London Diamond League—but her 2026 results have been inconsistent. She cleared 4.70 m indoors at All Star Perche (February) but struggled later in the indoor season (4.51 m in Rouen). Her outdoor 2026 season has no recorded competition yet, so she will rely on early momentum. A 4.58 m clearance would be solid but not enough to challenge the top tier.

**Emily Grove** (32) has not cleared above 4.55 m outdoors in 2026, with her best coming at the Drake Relays (4.55 m). She finished third in Zürich last year (4.75 m) but that form has not carried over. Her 2026 indoor best was 4.63 m, but she has struggled to translate that to outdoor meets. She will likely battle with Bonnin for the lower places, settling at 4.52 m.

**Marie-Julie Bonnin** (24) is the 2025 World Indoor champion, but her 2026 campaign has been disappointing. She managed only 4.00 m at a French club meet on 17 May, and her indoor season ended with a 7th-place 4.70 m at the World Indoors. Her outdoor 2025 Rabat result was also poor (4.35 m). The French athlete appears to be in a slump, and a 4.48 m clearance would be a modest rebound.

The battle for the top three will be intense, with Moon’s experience and Caudery’s youth leading the charge, while Šutej’s sterling indoor form makes her a podium threat. Ayris and Moser could disrupt the order if they produce career-best outdoor leaps, but the data points to a narrow Moon victory in a high-quality contest.

1. Muzala Samukonga (ZAM) – 44.01  
2. Zakithi Nene (RSA) – 44.25

9. Mohamed Yassine Zerhoumi (MAR) – 45.40  

---

### Race Preview and Reasoning

The 2026 Rabat Diamond League 400m brings together a deep field featuring the reigning Olympic champion, a world‑record holder in the European record‑book, and a young Zambian who has been the most in‑form man on the circuit this spring. Based on recent head‑to‑head results, seasonal trajectories and each athlete’s performance trends, the predicted order leans heavily on the Xiamen Diamond League meeting just eight days earlier (23 May 2026).

**Muzala Samukonga** arrives in Rabat as the clear favourite. His 44.04 in Xiamen – a season’s best and just 0.07 off his 2025 best – was the fastest time any man in this field has run this year. That race also saw him defeat Zakithi Nene by 0.36 seconds and Bayapo Ndori by 0.84, establishing a clear hierarchy. Samukonga, still only 23 and already a Commonwealth and Olympic bronze medallist, has improved his consistency this spring: he ran 44.55 in Nairobi, 44.83 in Tokyo and then that 44.04. His closing speed, honed by frequent 200m races (including a 20.23 this season), makes him particularly dangerous over the final 100m. A slight further sharpening for Rabat puts him in the 44.01 range.

**Zakithi Nene** has been remarkably solid: 44.50 in Nairobi, 44.44 in Florence and 44.40 in Xiamen. He has never been faster than Samukonga in any 2026 meeting, but his 44.40 in Xiamen was a respectable response after being beaten by Muzala. Nene’s 44.22 at the 2025 South African Championships and his 43.76 win in Nairobi last year show he has a higher gear, but he has not quite hit that level in 2026. Still, he is the second most consistent man in the field and should improve slightly in Rabat, perhaps to 44.25, especially with the motivation of a home‑continent crowd (though Rabat is North Africa, he’s a South African star). His 300m rust‑buster in Pretoria (31.85) hinted at good speed endurance.

**Jacory Patterson** won the 2025 Rabat Diamond League in 44.37, beating Nene by 0.09, and later that year ran 43.85 in Zurich. However, his 2026 outdoor form is less certain: his only open 400m was 44.41 in Melbourne (28 March), and he has raced mostly 200m since. That 44.41 is still a legitimate Diamond League‑calibre time, and Patterson has a proven ability to peak for one‑off races. He also has a strong tactical brain – witness his 43.98 at Grand Slam Track Miami last year. I expect him to run closer to 44.34, slotting behind Nene but ahead of the older stars.

**Matthew Hudson-Smith** is the most decorated man in the field (European record 43.44, Olympic silver, World silver) but his 2026 campaign has been deliberately light. He ran only one 400m before Rabat – a modest 45.39 at LSU in late April – and then focused on a 200m (20.51) in early May. At 31, he may be preserving his legs for the summer but cannot be written off. His pedigree suggests he can drop to 44.40 with a solid execution, especially on a Rabat track where he has raced well in the past (though he wasn’t in the 2025 edition). The lack of recent high‑level 400m reps, however, means he may lack the closing surge to challenge the top three.

**Khaleb McRae** is the reigning US indoor champion and ran an indoor 44.52 in February – faster than the ratified world indoor record. Outdoor, his last open 400m was a 43.91 win in Canada last summer, and he ran 44.16 in Budapest. Yet he has no 2026 outdoor 400m result to judge his form. Given his indoor prowess and strong relay work (2:57.33 in April), he should be in the low‑44s, but I see him slightly behind Hudson-Smith due to the British veteran’s greater big‑race experience. 44.42 is a reasonable estimate.

**Quincy Hall** is the defending Olympic champion but has not raced a 400m since June 2025 – nearly a year ago. That race was a 44.22 win in Rome, but his 2025 season also included a 45.99 in Shaoxing and a 44.90 in Rabat. Without recent competitive sharpness, he is a wild card. He could surprise, but the logical projection is a rusty 44.55, well off his Olympic gold form. The three‑year age gap (27) is not a factor, but the lack of rhythm is.

**Bayapo Ndori** – bronze medallist at the 2025 World Championships (44.20) – has struggled in 2026. His 44.88 in Xiamen was a season’s best but well behind Samukonga and Nene, and he was 5th in that race. He also ran 44.69 and 44.62 at Botswana Championships, indicating he is stuck in the mid‑44s. At 26, he should be in his prime, but the dip in form is real. I see him edging slightly better (44.80) but still off the top tier.

**Attila Molnár** – European indoor record holder – ran 45.49 in Xiamen, well behind the pack. He had a strong 2025 (44.74 in Budapest, 44.02 in Zurich promotional), but 2026 has not been kind outdoors. His 45.25 at the European Indoors was solid, but the flat outdoor pace suggests he is still adjusting. 45.25 is a fair prediction, placing him eighth.

**Mohamed Yassine Zerhoumi** – the local Moroccan – is a clear outsider. His best 2026 result is 45.03 in the African Championships heats, but he faded to 45.23 in the final. That is a second slower than the next‑slowest man (Molnár). He will have home support but lacks the raw speed to stay with this elite group. 45.40 is optimistic for him.

**Summary**  
The race will likely be decided by the form man Samukonga, who has the most recent high‑quality run (44.04) and the youth to back it up. Nene and Patterson provide the strongest chase, while Hudson‑Smith and McRae need a few more races to reach peak sharpness. Hall’s absence from competition puts him behind the proven 2026 performers. Ndori, Molnár and Zerhoumi round out the field with times reflecting their current struggles.
